title: Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being
authority: Ryan and Deci are the founders of self-determination theory; this is its canonical short statement.
caveats: Cross-cultural and applied support is strong for the three needs, but the theory is broad and some predictions (e.g. a strict continuum of regulation types) are debated. DOI, volume and pages cleared pending web confirmation.

title: A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation
authority: Meta-analysis of 128 experiments by leading SDT researchers, published in the top review journal in psychology.
caveats: Cameron and Pierce (1994) and Eisenberger and Cameron (1996) argued the undermining effect is small and avoidable; Deci et al. rebutted. Most studies measure free-choice behavior in brief lab tasks, often with children or undergraduates. Effects on interesting tasks only; rewards for dull tasks do not undermine.

title: Undermining children's intrinsic interest with extrinsic reward: A test of the overjustification hypothesis
container: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
authority: The founding experiment of the overjustification effect, by Stanford social psychologists.
caveats: Small preschool sample, one task (felt-tip pens), one session. Boundary conditions found later: unexpected rewards, informational (competence-affirming) feedback and rewards for uninteresting tasks do not undermine. DOI, volume and pages cleared pending web confirmation.

title: Flow: The psychology of optimal experience
authority: Csikszentmihalyi originated flow research at the University of Chicago and Claremont; this is the canonical book statement (first paper-length account in Beyond Boredom and Anxiety, 1975).
caveats: Much evidence is from the Experience Sampling Method and self-report; the challenge-skill balance prediction has mixed support and the construct is hard to measure without disrupting it. Flow in games is often over-claimed. DOI, volume and pages cleared pending web confirmation.

title: Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change
authority: Bandura is among the most cited psychologists; this paper introduced self-efficacy.
caveats: Meta-analyses (Stajkovic and Luthans 1998; Multon et al. 1991) show moderate efficacy-performance correlations, but causal direction is partly reciprocal (performance raises efficacy). Early evidence relied on phobia treatment. DOI, volume and pages cleared pending web confirmation.

title: Building a practically useful theory of goal setting and task motivation: A 35-year odyssey
authority: Locke and Latham are the originators of goal-setting theory; this is their summary of 35 years of research.
caveats: Critics (Ordonez, Schweitzer, Galinsky, Bazerman 2009, 'Goals Gone Wild') document harms of narrow or overly ambitious goals; effects strongest for simple tasks and weaker for complex new learning where learning goals are better than performance goals. DOI, volume and pages cleared pending web confirmation.

title: The progress principle: Using small wins to ignite joy, engagement, and creativity at work
authority: Amabile is a Harvard Business School professor and leading creativity researcher; the book reports a multi-year diary study.
caveats: Workplace sample, self-reported diaries, correlational; popular framing is stronger than the data. Generalization to voluntary learners is plausible but untested. DOI, volume and pages cleared pending web confirmation.

title: The goal-gradient hypothesis resurrected: Purchase acceleration, illusionary goal progress, and customer retention
authority: Peer-reviewed field and lab evidence in a top marketing journal reviving Hull's 1932 goal-gradient hypothesis.
caveats: Commercial loyalty contexts (coffee cards, music rewards), not education. Effort may drop sharply after reward receipt. Replication across domains is reasonable but not exhaustive. DOI, volume and pages cleared pending web confirmation.

title: The endowed progress effect: How artificial advancement increases effort
authority: Field experiment in a leading consumer research journal.
caveats: One field study with a car wash plus lab studies; later work (e.g. Bonezzi, Brendl, De Angelis 2011; Hsee et al. 2013 'medium maximization') shows boundary conditions. Artificial advancement can feel manipulative if the head start is not justified. DOI, volume and pages cleared pending web confirmation.

title: Does gamification work? A literature review of empirical studies on gamification
container: Proceedings of the 47th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences
authority: The most cited early systematic review of gamification, by Finnish information systems researchers.
caveats: Reviewed 24 studies, mostly short, small and uncontrolled; authors concluded positive but context-dependent effects and flagged novelty effect and poor methodology. DOI, volume and pages cleared pending web confirmation.

title: The gamification of learning: A meta-analysis
authority: Peer-reviewed meta-analysis of experimental and quasi-experimental studies from LMU Munich researchers.
caveats: High heterogeneity; motivational and behavioral effects were less stable than cognitive ones when only rigorous studies were kept. Gamification is a bundle, so effects cannot be assigned to single elements.

title: Assessing the effects of gamification in the classroom: A longitudinal study on intrinsic motivation, social comparison, satisfaction, effort, and academic performance
authority: Peer-reviewed longitudinal classroom study, a frequently cited cautionary result.
caveats: Single course, roughly 80 students, one implementation (leaderboard plus badges). Not a refutation of all gamification, but a warning about competitive designs. DOI, volume and pages cleared pending web confirmation.

title: A motivational model of video game engagement
authority: Applies self-determination theory to games; introduces the PENS measure; authors include SDT co-founder Ryan.
caveats: Survey and experimental work with mostly young adult gamers; self-report; correlational for many links. DOI, volume and pages cleared pending web confirmation.

title: How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world
authority: UCL health psychology study, the standard citation for habit-formation timelines.
caveats: 96 volunteers, simple health behaviors, self-reported automaticity; the 66-day median applies to a modelled subset and the range is 18 to 254 days. The popular 21-day claim has no evidence.

title: To what extent and under which circumstances are growth mind-sets important to academic achievement? Two meta-analyses
authority: Large pre-registered-style meta-analyses of mindset correlations and interventions; the main critical counterweight to popular mindset claims (see Yeager et al. 2019 Nature for a positive, calibrated reading).
caveats: Dweck's group argues the meta-analysis pooled heterogeneous interventions; Yeager et al. 2019 found small but real effects for low achievers in a large randomized trial. DOI, volume and pages cleared pending web confirmation.
